--------------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Block-level Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Why DID?  
• The reform produced an abrupt, plausibly exogenous increase in fixed, uniformed police on only a subset of blocks (those hosting Jewish/Muslim institutions).  
• We observe the same blocks before and after 25 July 1994 as well as untreated blocks in the same neighborhoods over the same window, giving us panel variation in treatment and time.  
• DID absorbs all time-invariant block attributes (street layout, socio-economic composition, parking supply, etc.) and any city-wide shocks in a common time effect.  
• A flexible event-study version (leads/lags) lets us test pre-trend equality and study dynamic displacement.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 if block i hosts a Jewish/Muslim institution that received 24-hour police protection *and* t ≥ 25 July 1994; 0 otherwise.

Intensity / spillover bins (for heterogeneous-effects analysis)  
TR0  Control  (≥3 blocks away)  
TR1  Same block (fixed post)  
TR2  1 block away  
TR3  2 blocks away  

Control group  
Blocks in the same three neighborhoods that are ≥3 blocks from any protected institution.

Timing  
• Pre-period: 1 Apr – 24 Jul 1994  
• Post-period: 25 Jul – 31 Dec 1994  
We aggregate to months by default (weekly data used for robustness / event study).

No running variable or cutoff is involved; hence RDD is not applicable.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the reform, crime on treated and control blocks would have evolved similarly.  
   – Plausible because locations of Jewish institutions were fixed decades earlier and not chosen for crime reasons.  
   – Testable with event-study coefficients on pre-treatment lags.

A2. No simultaneous shocks differentially affecting treated blocks exactly at 25 Jul.  
   – Plausible; the bombing led only to policing changes. There was no contemporaneous local redevelopment, street closure, insurance change, etc.

A3. Stable reporting/measurement: The probability that a theft is reported does not jump differentially on treated blocks.  
   – Because theft victims file at local precincts irrespective of the street’s police post, reporting incentives should not dramatically change. We can indirectly test by examining violent vs. non-violent theft or vandalism as placebo outcomes.

A4. SUTVA / no interference across units beyond the spillovers we model.  
   – Spatial displacement is a concern; we explicitly estimate effects on 1- and 2-block rings, which is the relevant interference channel.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
------------------------------------------------
T1. Crime displacement within neighborhoods  
   – Include distance rings to measure deterrence vs. displacement.  
   – Conduct neighborhood-month fixed effects; compare net change across rings to test for redistribution.

T2. Endogenous police redeployment elsewhere (baseline patrol reduction)  
   – Because posts were staffed by pulling officers from administrative units, not from neighborhood patrols, the threat is limited. We will nevertheless include neighborhood×time fixed effects to absorb any neighborhood-wide patrol changes.

T3. Differential seasonality (winter vs. summer) interacting with streets that host synagogues (e.g., attendance patterns)  
   – Month fixed effects common to all blocks remove city-wide seasonality.  
   – Pre-period seasonality check: plot May–July trends for 1993 from archival data, if available, or show flat pre-trends within 1994.

5. R CODE OUTLINE
------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast DID / Poisson
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & merge data ----------------------------------------------
crime   <- fread("block_week_crime.csv")        # one row per block-week
blocks  <- fread("block_covariates.csv")        # census fractions, distance cat.
distmat <- fread("block_distance_to_temple.csv")# same, 1-block, 2-block, ≥3

dt <- merge(crime, blocks, by = "block_id")
dt <- merge(dt, distmat, by = "block_id")

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------
# Treatment categories
dt[, treat_block  := (dist_cat == "same")]        # same block
dt[, ring1_block  := (dist_cat == "1away")]       # 1 block
dt[, ring2_block  := (dist_cat == "2away")]       # 2 blocks
dt[, control_block:= (dist_cat == ">=3")]         # ≥3 blocks

# Post indicator (week >= 30 implies ≥ 25 July 1994)
dt[, post := (date >= as.Date("1994-07-25"))]

# DID treatment indicator
dt[, treat := treat_block * post]

# Event study leads/lags in weeks
ref_date <- as.Date("1994-07-25")
dt[, rel_week := as.integer((date - ref_date)/7)]
for (k in -12:22) dt[, paste0("D",k) := (rel_week==k)]

# 3. Main specification (Poisson with two-way FE) --------------------
feols_main <- feglm(
  thefts ~ treat | block_id + week,
  data  = dt,
  family=poisson(),           # count outcome
  cluster = ~block_id         # cluster at block level
)
summary(feols_main)

# 4. Heterogeneous effects / spillovers ------------------------------
dt[, post_x_ring1 := ring1_block * post]
dt[, post_x_ring2 := ring2_block * post]
dt[, post_x_control := 0] # baseline

feols_ring <- feglm(
  thefts ~ treat + post_x_ring1 + post_x_ring2 | block_id + week,
  data = dt, family = poisson(), cluster = ~block_id)
summary(feols_ring)

# 5. Event-study graph (pre-trend test) ------------------------------
est <- feglm(thefts ~ D-12 + D-11 + ... + D22 | block_id + week,
             data = dt, family=poisson(), cluster=~block_id)

beta  <- coef(est)[paste0("D", -12:22)]
se    <- sqrt(diag(vcov(est)))[paste0("D", -12:22)]
ggplot(data.frame(w=-12:22, b=beta, se=se),
       aes(x=w, y=b)) +
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=b-1.96*se, ymax=b+1.96*se)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept= -0.5, linetype="dashed") +
  labs(x="Weeks relative to police deployment", y="Log theft change")

# 6. Robustness: block-specific linear trends ------------------------
dt[, trend := as.numeric(week)]
feols_trend <- feglm(
  thefts ~ treat | block_id[trend] + week,
  data = dt, family = poisson(), cluster = ~block_id)
summary(feols_trend)
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS
------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Becker, deterrence) predicts a fall in property crime where the perceived probability of apprehension rises. Because the post is continuous and visible, I expect a sizeable deterrence:

• Same-block effect: −35 % to −45 % in the theft rate (IRR ≈ 0.55–0.65)  
• 1-block ring: modest −10 % to −15 % (IRR ≈ 0.85–0.9) or zero if thieves simply shift.  
• 2-block ring and beyond: zero or slight increase if substitution occurs.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)
------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-trend parallel (shown by event-study) .................... 1  
C2: No differential contemporaneous shocks ....................... 1  
C3: No systematic treatment mis-classification ................... 1  
C4: Limited spillovers / SUTVA (modelled with rings) ............. 0.5  
C5: Stable outcome measurement ................................... 0.8  

Overall: 4.3 / 5 → design appears high-quality but depends on documented flat pre-trends and bounded displacement.
